doc.headline: Use {arm:brisk-s.low.r1}: the cheapest configuration to clear the {criteria.pass_rate.threshold} pass-rate gate, though only by {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.overall.distance|abs} points.
doc.lede: It costs {cost_per_1k.brisk-s.low.r1} per 1k calls, least of the {count.passing.pass_rate|words} that clear, but a fresh run of today's size reads it below the gate {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.overall.wrong_side} of the time. If the gate must clear with confidence, high reasoning (L) is the pick, at {cost_per_1k.brisk-s.high.r1} per 1k calls.

caveats.material_if: If J's true pass rate sits below the gate, which its clearance of {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.overall.distance|abs} points cannot rule out, then L is the cheapest configuration that clears; settling J four times in five would take {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.overall.cases_needed_two_sided_80} cases, two-sided.

J's figure is partly the luck of being picked from {n_candidates} configurations: a run on fresh cases tends to read it lower, which pushes it toward or under the gate and leaves L, with {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.overall.distance|abs} points of room, as the pick.

Only for a claim that one configuration beats another on pass rate: every gap here is read unpaired and so wider than a paired reading; the call rests on each configuration's own gate reading and its cost.

caveats.label: Cost routing unknown
caveats.material_if: Only if another provider's pricing for Brisk-S or Atlas-M reorders them: the snapshot names the model each arm served but no provider, so every cost is this run's routing's, not the model's own.

decision.text: Ship {arm:brisk-s.low.r1}. It reads {measure.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.mean} against the {criteria.pass_rate.threshold} gate at {cost_per_1k.brisk-s.low.r1} per 1k calls, the least of any configuration that clears: about {cost_per_month.brisk-s.low.r1} a month if the declared volume counts calls, more if it counts tasks, by each arm's calls per task.

{arm:brisk-s.high.r1} clears with more room, {measure.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.mean}, but costs {cost_per_1k.brisk-s.high.r1} per 1k calls, {price.brisk-s.low.r1.brisk-s.high.r1.pass_rate.monthly_cost_gap|abs} more a month if the volume counts calls. Every Atlas-M that clears costs more again; the best, {arm:atlas-m.high.r1}, reads {measure.pass_rate.atlas-m.high.r1.mean} at {cost_per_1k.atlas-m.high.r1} per 1k calls. No Nano-XS configuration clears; its best, {arm:nano-xs.high.r1}, falls {criteria.pass_rate.nano-xs.high.r1.gap|abs} points short.

The weakest margin is the pick's own: {weakest.arm} reads {weakest.value} on {weakest.criterion} against {weakest.threshold}. A fresh run of today's size reads it below the line {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.overall.wrong_side} of the time, against {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.overall.wrong_side} for L, and as the best of {n_candidates} it likely reads high.
Ship J now; in parallel the planner's owner declares whether the gate must clear on its interval. If it must, switch to L.

claims.text: Only {count.passing.pass_rate|words} of {n_candidates|words} configurations clear the {criteria.pass_rate.threshold} gate, and J sits closest to the line at {measure.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.mean}.

evidence.caption: Each configuration's pass rate with a computed interval, against the gate at {criteria.pass_rate.threshold}; J is stressed.

claims.text: Of the configurations that clear, J costs least: {cost_per_1k.brisk-s.low.r1} per 1k calls, against {cost_per_1k.brisk-s.high.r1} for L and {cost_per_1k.atlas-m.low.r1} for the cheapest Atlas-M.

evidence.caption: Cost per 1k calls of the configurations that clear the gate, on a log scale, at this run's provider routing, which the snapshot does not name.

claims.text: J's clearance is inside its noise: a fresh run of today's size would read it below the gate {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.overall.wrong_side} of the time, against {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.overall.wrong_side} for L. A two-sided run that settles it four times in five needs {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.overall.cases_needed_two_sided_80} cases for J and {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.overall.cases_needed_two_sided_80} for L.

evidence.caption: Distance to the gate, how often a run of today's size reads the other side, and the cases that settle the line half the time; the four-in-five, two-sided sizes cited above are larger: {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.overall.cases_needed_two_sided_80} for J and {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.overall.cases_needed_two_sided_80} for L.

claims.text: High reasoning adds {compare.brisk-s.high.r1.brisk-s.low.r1.pass_rate.overall.difference} points over low, an interval of {compare.brisk-s.high.r1.brisk-s.low.r1.pass_rate.overall.interval} that does not exclude zero, for {cost_per_1k.brisk-s.high.r1} against {cost_per_1k.brisk-s.low.r1} per 1k calls.

evidence.caption: L minus J on pass rate, overall with an unpaired interval; the per-task rows state no case counts, so they carry no interval and are descriptive only.

claims.text: The retry is what lifts J over the gate: it adds {lever.retry.brisk-s.low.r0.brisk-s.low.r1.pass_rate.effect} points to Brisk-S at low reasoning, an interval of {lever.retry.brisk-s.low.r0.brisk-s.low.r1.pass_rate.interval}.

evidence.caption: What reasoning and the retry each add to Brisk-S's pass rate along the moves that lead to J and L, with unpaired intervals; the interaction shown is not separated from zero.

explore.binds: Which configuration is the cheapest that clears
explore.outcome: J stays the pick for a gate above {criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r0.value} up to {criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.value}; L from there up to {criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.value}; {arm:atlas-m.high.r1} up to {criteria.pass_rate.atlas-m.high.r1.value}; above that nothing clears. Lower gates admit cheaper Brisk-S and Nano-XS configurations.

explore.control: Reading the gate on the interval rather than the point estimate
explore.outcome: J's computed interval crosses the gate while L's sits above it, so on the interval L becomes the pick at {cost_per_1k.brisk-s.high.r1} per 1k calls against {cost_per_1k.brisk-s.low.r1}; a month that is {price.brisk-s.low.r1.brisk-s.high.r1.pass_rate.monthly_cost_gap|abs} more if the volume counts calls, more if it counts tasks.

omitted.why: No latency gate was declared, and latency does not reorder the two Brisk-S options; full figures in the appendix.
Varies little between the options a decider would weigh and changes no gate reading; it matters only to what a month costs if the volume counts tasks, which the cost lines say.

omitted.what: Extra calls per task and outcome
omitted.why: The snapshot holds no figures for either.

omitted.what: Per-task pass rates of the other configurations
omitted.why: The gate reads overall; per-task figures state no case counts, so they are leads, kept in the appendix.

omitted.what: Model and reasoning lever effects across Atlas-M and Nano-XS, and the high-reasoning retry move for Brisk-S
omitted.why: They explain why other configurations fall short or cost more but do not change the pick; all are in the appendix.

next.text: The planner's owner declares whether the gate must clear on its interval or on its point estimate.
next.settles: Whether J ships or L does: more cases cannot practically settle J, which would need {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.overall.cases_needed_two_sided_80} cases to settle four times in five, two-sided.

next.text: Add worked multi-hop examples to Brisk-S's planning prompt, where J reads {task.multihop.brisk-s.low.r1.pass_rate.mean} (a figure with no stated case count, so no interval), then re-run J on {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.overall.cases_needed_two_sided_80} fresh cases.
next.settles: Whether the change lifts J clear of the gate at its current cost: a run that size settles a clearance as large as L's, {settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.overall.distance|abs} points, four times in five; a smaller lift needs more cases.

Whether L's clearance survives fresh cases. The size assumes today's estimate of {measure.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.mean}; the best-of-many selection likely reads that high, and a lower true rate needs more cases to settle four times in five.

next.text: Declare each task's traffic share and case count, and whether the monthly volume counts calls or tasks.
next.settles: Whether the overall pass rate reflects the production mix, and what the step from J to L costs a month.

method.text: Each configuration ran {scoreboard.brisk-s.low.r1.cases} cases once each across the task types; none was lost or failed to run. Per-task case counts are not stated.
The input does not define what makes a planner run pass.
Pass rate at least {criteria.pass_rate.threshold}, declared before the run and read on each configuration's point estimate, as declared.

Computed here from each configuration's cases as a binomial spread by the normal approximation, at the level each block prints. Gaps between configurations are unpaired, since no control was run, and uncorrected for the number of comparisons. Run sizes are quoted two-sided, sized to settle four times in five unless a table says otherwise.

Cost per 1k calls as measured. Each arm names its model but no provider. Monthly figures use the declared volume of {meta.volume_per_month} read as calls; the input does not say whether it counts calls or tasks, and if it counts tasks each monthly figure grows by the arm's calls per task.
The pick is the cheapest of {n_candidates} configurations to clear the gate, so its pass rate likely reads high.

items.name: First screen
items.reason: The headline, lede and decision block tell a reader what to ship (Brisk-S, low reasoning, one retry), why (it costs least of the five that clear, at $0.302 per 1k calls) and the main risk (it clears by only 0.1 points, and a fresh run reads it below the gate 38.6% of the time). They also name the safer pick (high reasoning, at $1,324 more a month). c1 backs this: five of eighteen clear, and the pick sits closest to the line. options_dominance agrees that the pick is the only undominated survivor.

items.name: Coherent story
items.reason: The claims follow on from one another. c1 shows who clears, c2 prices them, c3 shows how thin the margin is, and c4 and c5 explain what buys pass rate. Each claim matches its block row by row. The figures check out: settle_cases gives 38.6% and 0.9%, and the threshold sweep gives the pick's band as 95.3% to 97.1%. But the first confidence bullet says the pick's 'true pass rate sits below the gate'. That contradicts the headline and c3, which estimate it at 97.1%, above the line, and only call the clearance inside the noise.

items.name: Honest emphasis
items.reason: The pick's weak axis, its 0.1-point clearance, is in the headline, Watch, c3 and a Low confidence. c4 says the high-over-low gain of +0.8 (-0.4 to +2.1) does not exclude zero. The only overreach is minor: c4's caption ranks per-task gains that have no interval.

items.name: Sound elision
items.reason: Nothing left out would change the call. Latency favours the pick (513 ms p95, against 870 ms for high reasoning). Calls per task are similar (1.539 against 1.476) and don't reorder the cost. The per-task rates are in the appendix and in a next step.

items.name: Confounds handled
items.reason: No control, best-of-18 selection and unnamed cost routing are each carried in a confidence clause and a next step. The ambiguity over the volume unit is in Method and a next step, but the headline, decision and explore state '$1,324 more a month' flatly. If the 4,000,000 counts tasks, the gap is about $1,880 a month, from each arm's calls per task. A reader pricing the trade could be misled by about 40%.

items.name: Actionable next steps
items.reason: Declaring how the gate reads, re-running high reasoning on 1,660 cases and declaring traffic shares are concrete, and each says what it settles. 'Improve Brisk-S's multi-hop planning and re-run J' names neither the change nor a run size, so it settles nothing in particular.

items.name: Evidence fits claims
items.reason: c1, c2, c4 and c5 each show their claim's figure. But the page's headline settling numbers, 111,255 cases for the pick and 1,660 for high reasoning, are not in c3's block. That block prints 38,350 and 54,451 for the pick, and 572 and 812 for high reasoning. A reader sees two different 'cases to settle' figures for the same arm with no link between them. c5 prints one interval end as '+0.03535'.

findings.finding: The first confidence bullet reads 'J's true pass rate sits below the gate'. That asserts the pick fails, which contradicts the headline and c3: the estimate is 97.1%, above the 97% line, and the clearance is only inside its noise. Reword it as a condition, for example: 'If J's true pass rate sits below the gate, which its 0.1-point clearance cannot rule out, then L is the cheapest configuration that clears.'

The confidence line and next steps cite 111,255 cases to settle the pick and 1,660 for high reasoning 'four times in five'. Those are the two-sided sizes at four-in-five, settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.overall.cases_needed_two_sided_80 and settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.overall.cases_needed_two_sided_80. c3's block shows only the half-of-runs sizes: 38,350 and 54,451 for the pick, and 572 and 812 for high reasoning. Add the four-in-five columns to c3's table, or label in the text which size each number is, so a reader doesn't see two unexplained case counts for the same arm.

The headline, decision ('about $1,208 a month', '$1,324 more a month', '$11,376 a month more than L') and the explore row price the trade as if the 4,000,000 monthly volume counts calls. Method says the input doesn't say whether it counts calls or tasks. If it counts tasks, each figure scales by calls per task (1.539 for the pick, 1.476 for high reasoning), and the gap becomes about $1,880 a month. Qualify the monthly figures with 'if the volume counts calls', or give both readings, where the trade is priced.

The second next step, 'Improve Brisk-S's multi-hop planning, where J reads 95.6%, and re-run J', names no specific change and no run size. Name the intervention, such as a prompt or tool change for multi-hop. Give the cases a re-run would need to show the pick clears with room, and note that per-task case counts are unstated, so the 95.6% has no interval.

The third next step sizes the high-reasoning re-run at 1,660 cases on today's 98.0%. The page itself says best-of-18 selection makes today's figures read high, and if the truth is lower that size settles it less than four times in five. Say that the size assumes today's estimate, or size it on a lower plausible pass rate.

The caption says 'multi-hop gains the most' (+1.7, against +0.1 to +1.2 elsewhere). The per-task rows carry no interval because per-task case counts are unstated. Mark the per-task ordering as descriptive, or drop the ranking from the caption.

The retry effect for Brisk-S at high reasoning prints its interval as '+0.03535 to +2.6'. Every other end is at one decimal place. Round it to match (+0.04 or +0.0) so it doesn't read as false precision.

items.name: First screen
items.reason: The headline, lede and decision block say what to do: ship Brisk-S at low reasoning with 1 retry (J), at $0.302 per 1k calls. They say why: it is the cheapest of the five configurations that clear the gate. And they say the main risk: it clears by only 0.1 points, and a fresh run of today's size would read it below the gate 38.6% of the time. The fallback is named with its price: Brisk-S at high reasoning with 1 retry (L), at $0.633. c1 shows the five that clear, with J closest to the line. options_dominance agrees that J is the only undominated option.

items.name: Coherent story
items.reason: Each claim leads to the next. c1 shows who clears, c2 shows J costs least among them, and c3 shows J's clearance is inside its noise. c4 shows L's gain over J is not separated from zero, and c5 shows the retry is what lifts J over the line. I checked each sentence against its block, row by row, and found no conflict. The gap +0.8 (-0.4 to +2.1), the retry effect +1.9 (+0.3 to +3.4), the 38.6% and 0.9% wrong-side shares, and the 111,255 and 1,660 two-sided four-in-five sizes all match the snapshot. In the explore row, the gate ranges (J above 95.3% up to 97.1%, L up to 98%, F up to 98.6%) follow from the table. Last round's conflict in the confidence bullet is fixed: it now reads as a condition ('If J's true pass rate sits below the gate...').

items.name: Honest emphasis
items.reason: The pick's weak axis is the headline's own qualifier, and it shows again in Watch, in c3 and in the Low confidence. Best-of-18 selection is named as pushing J's figure high. The monthly figures ('about $1,208', '$1,324 more') now say they assume the volume counts calls and would be larger if it counts tasks. Last round's should_fix on this is resolved. c4's caption now marks the per-task rows as descriptive, which resolves the ranking finding.

items.name: Sound elision
items.reason: None of the omitted items changes the call. Latency favours J (513 ms p95 against 870 ms for L) and has no gate. Calls per task are close (1.539 against 1.476) and are named in the monthly-cost qualifier. Dropping the high-reasoning retry effect from c5 also removes the badly rounded interval end flagged last round. That row is not on the path to J.

items.name: Confounds handled
items.reason: All three caveats the snapshot lists are carried, each with a statement of when it would matter: point-estimate clearance, best of 18, and no control. Each has a next step: declare whether the gate reads on its interval, and re-run L at a size the page says assumes today's 98.0%. Unknown cost routing is named in the confidence line, in c2's caveat and caption, and in Method, which answers the cost_served_by fact: the snapshot names no provider, and the page says every cost is this run's routing's. Unstated per-task counts and traffic mix have their own declaration step.

items.name: Actionable next steps
items.reason: Each step names an action and what it settles. One is the owner's declaration on reading the gate, which decides J against L. One adds worked multi-hop examples to the planning prompt and re-runs J on 1,660 cases, with the size's reach stated. One re-runs L on 1,660 cases, noting that the size assumes today's estimate. One declares traffic shares and the volume unit. All three next-step findings from last round are resolved.

items.name: Evidence fits claims
items.reason: Each block draws its claim's figure. c1 is a dot-interval against the gate line. c2 is cost bars for the configurations that clear, on a log scale, as its caption says. c4 shows the overall gap with its interval and labels the per-task rows descriptive. c5 shows the retry move with its interval. c3's table shows the half-of-runs sizes, and its caption now labels the four-in-five, two-sided sizes the text cites, which answers last round's finding. The counterfactual holds: if J's row fell below 97%, c1 and the headline would have to change.
